title: Footballs for a global brand
body: A large sports goods company based in Europe sells footballs under its own famous brand name in more than fifty countries. It does not own any factory in India. Instead, it places large orders with hundreds of small producers in and around Jalandhar, many of whom stitch the balls at home with the help of family members. The company decides the design, the quality checks, the delivery dates and the price it will pay for each ball. If the small producers ask for a higher price, the company's buyers point out that producers in other countries are ready to supply the same balls for less. The finished balls are collected, packed and shipped abroad, where they are sold at many times the price paid to the producers.

title: A small switch-maker under pressure
body: Meena took a bank loan in the mid-1990s to start a small unit making electrical switches in an industrial town. Her main buyers were Indian companies that made household appliances. Within a few years she employed 25 workers. After the government removed restrictions on imports of such components, her buyers began to import switches that cost about half of what she charged. Some of the appliance companies themselves started only assembling products for MNC brands. Meena's orders fell sharply; she now employs only eight workers, and several units in her town have closed. She says her machines are old, power cuts are frequent, and she cannot get a fresh loan at a reasonable rate of interest to modernise.
